bibl.title: The Anatomy of the Facebook Social Graph

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: First, we characterize the global structure of the graph, determining that the social network is nearly fully connected, with 99.91% of individuals belonging to a single large connected component, and we confirm the ‘six degrees of separation’ phenomenon on a global scale.

span.label: structure of the Facebook social graph
span.quote: In this work, we characterize the structure of the world’s largest online social network, Facebook, in an effort to advance the state of the art in the empirical study of social networks.

span.label: large-scale-network-analysis
span.quote: Unless otherwise noted, calculations were performed on a Hadoop cluster with 2,250 machines, using the Hadoop/Hive data analysis framework developed at Facebook [45, 46].

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the population is fixed by a STIPULATED definition of an active user - logged in within the last 28 days AND holding at least one friend - and the authors state that this is not the platform's own definition and that their statistics therefore differ from company figures
span.quote: We defined a user of Facebook as an active member of the social network if they logged into the site in the last 28 days from our time of measurement in May 2011 and had at least one Facebook friend. We note that this definition is not precisely Facebook’s ordinary definition of active user, and therefore some of our statistics differ slightly from company statistics.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the whole graph is analysed rather than sampled or crawled, and the stated reason is a defect of the alternatives rather than a preference: sampling and crawling cannot tell an active account from a stale one
span.quote: Then another thread of research has measured some large-scale network properties of the Facebook graph through sampling, crawling, and other methods to collect network data [22,23]. Notably, these methodologies have no way of distinguishing between active and stale accounts. Unlike these studies, we analyze the entire Facebook graph in anonymized form and focus on the set of active user accounts reliably corresponding to people.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the neighbourhood function is used in place of the diameter, because the diameter is an extremal measure that a single ill-connected path in a peripheral region can wildly distort, while a percentile of vertex pairs is robust to it
span.quote: The diameter is an extremal measure, and it is commonly considered less interesting than the full neighborhood function, which measures what percentile of vertex pairs are within a given distance. The exact diameter can be wildly distorted by the presence of a single ill-connected path in some peripheral region of the graph, while the neighborhood function and its average are thought to robustly capture the ‘typical’ distances between pairs of vertices.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the paper rejects the power-law model for its degree distribution and then DECLINES to fit a replacement, naming instead the features of the distribution it takes to be the relevant results
span.quote: We conclude, like Ref. [23], that strict power-law models are inappropriate for Facebook’s degree distribution. It is not our intent, though, to determine which parametric form best models the distribution. The relevant results are the monotonicity and curvature of the degree distribution, the degrees of typical users, the large variance in degrees, and the network’s sparsity.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the component structure is computed by a union-find algorithm with path compression that records components as edges are added, which is chosen because IT DOES NOT REQUIRE THE EDGES TO BE HELD IN MEMORY - the whole edge list is streamed past a single machine instead
span.quote: The NZ algorithm, a type of Union-Find algorithm with path compression, records component structure dynamically as edges are added to a network that begins completely empty of edges. When all edges are added, the algorithm has computed the component structure of the network. Crucially for our purposes, the NZ algorithm does not require the edges to be retained in memory. We apply it to the Facebook network on a single computer with 64GB of RAM by streaming over the list of edges.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: neighbourhood statistics are estimated from a stratified sample rather than the whole graph: users are drawn by reservoir sampling at each of a hundred log-spaced neighbourhood sizes, and the reported percentiles are stated to be empirical percentiles of that sample rather than of the population
span.quote: For analyzing network neighborhoods, 5,000 users were randomly selected using reservoir sampling for each of 100 log-spaced neighborhood sizes, creating a sample of 500,000 users for which the analysis was performed. The percentiles shown for the clustering coefficient and degeneracy for each neighborhood size are therefore empirical percentiles from this sample population of 5,000 users.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the path-length figures are produced by running the neighbourhood-function algorithm repeatedly on one machine and AVERAGING ACROSS THE RUNS rather than computing once
span.quote: For path length calculations, neighborhood functions were computed on a single 24-core machine with 72 GB of RAM using the HyperANF algorithm [48], averaging across 10 runs.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the edge relation is restricted to RECIPROCAL friendships only, and the authors date the restriction: the analysis predated the existence of subscriptions on the platform
span.quote: Our analysis predated the existence of ‘subscriptions’ on Facebook, and in this work we study only reciprocal Facebook friendships.

span.label: The paper's own definition of an 'active' user departs from Facebook's, so its statistics differ from company figures.
span.note: what this limits: every comparison between this paper's statistics and Facebook's: THIS DEFINITION IS NOT PRECISELY FACEBOOK'S ORDINARY DEFINITION OF ACTIVE USER, AND THEREFORE SOME OF OUR STATISTICS DIFFER SLIGHTLY FROM COMPANY STATISTICS
span.quote: We note that this definition is not precisely Facebook’s ordinary definition of active user, and therefore some of our statistics differ slightly from company statistics.

span.label: Country assignment relies on geo-IP data, which is imperfect and only reliable at national granularity.
span.note: what this limits: any country-level result: country assignment relies on geo-IP data, imperfect and reliable only at national granularity
span.quote: While imperfect, so-called geo-IP data is generally reliable on a national level.

span.label: The analysis is acknowledged as non-exhaustive with respect to available network measures.
span.note: what this limits: the completeness of the structural picture: WE HAVE CERTAINLY NOT EXHAUSTED THE POSSIBILITIES OF NETWORK ANALYSIS
span.quote: While our computations have elucidated many aspects of the structure of the world’s largest social network, we have certainly not exhausted the possibilities of network analysis.

span.label: The 'six degrees' confirmation is a statement about percentages of pairs in a friendship graph, not a repeat of the experiment that produced the phrase.
span.note: what this limits: the claim that this work confirms six degrees of separation: what is reported is that 92% of all pairs of Facebook users were within five degrees and 99.6% within six, measured as shortest paths in the friendship graph
span.quote: As Figure 2 shows, fully 92% of all pairs of Facebook users were within five degrees of separation, and 99.6% were within six degrees

span.label: The object studied is an abstraction the authors themselves call limited.
span.note: what this limits: any social conclusion drawn from this graph: the authors describe the network abstraction of human relationships as certainly limited, while useful for characterising social relationships
span.quote: This abstract view of human relationships, while certainly limited, has been very useful for characterizing social relationships

span.label: A small group of accounts sits far outside the typical user, so the average describes nobody in particular.
span.note: what this limits: an average degree quoted from this paper: a small population of users with abnormally high degrees, called hubs in the networks literature, have degrees far larger than the average or median user
span.quote: The small population of users with abnormally high degrees, sometimes called hubs in the networks literature, have degrees far larger than the average or median Facebook user

span.label: Feld's friendship paradox - that your friends have more friends than you do - taken as the frame for reading the degree distribution of the whole Facebook graph
span.quote: Feld’s observation that ‘your friends have more friends than you’ is an important psychological paradox, applying to friendship as well as sexual partners.

span.label: the entire Facebook graph analysed in anonymised form rather than a sample, restricted to active accounts reliably corresponding to people
span.note: eliminates: sampling bias, which the paper names as the standing problem of online social network research - there is no sample to be unrepresentative of the whole when the whole is the data
span.quote: Unlike these studies, we analyze the entire Facebook graph in anonymized form and focus on the set of active user accounts reliably corresponding to people.

span.label: the structural results compared against those from smaller social networks
span.note: eliminates: a structural property that belongs to Facebook's scale or design rather than to social networks - and the comparison is reported as agreeing only in part
span.quote: We compare our results with those from smaller social networks and find mostly, but not entirely, agreement on common structural network characteristics.

span.label: active user
span.quote: Unlike these studies, we analyze the entire Facebook graph in anonymized form and focus on the set of active user accounts reliably corresponding to people. We defined a user of Facebook as an active member of the social network if they logged into the site in the last 28 days from our time of measurement in May 2011 and had at least one Facebook friend

span.label: degrees of separation
span.quote: As Figure 2 shows, fully 92% of all pairs of Facebook users were within five degrees of separation, and 99.6% were within six degrees

span.label: short path lengths
span.quote: Short path lengths between individuals, the so-called “six degrees of separation” found by Stanley Milgram’s experiments investigating the social network of the United States [26], are here seen in Facebook on a global scale

span.label: local clustering coefficient
span.quote: for users with 100 friends, the average local clustering coefficient is 0.14, indicating that for a median user, 14% of all their friend pairs are themselves friends

span.label: hubs
span.quote: The small population of users with abnormally high degrees, sometimes called hubs in the networks literature

span.label: 'active user' - STIPULATED, AND EXPLICITLY NOT THE PLATFORM'S: logged in within 28 days and holding at least one friend, which the authors state is not Facebook's ordinary definition and is why their statistics differ from the company's; the 721 million figure counts exactly what this sentence picks out
span.quote: We defined a user of Facebook as an active member of the social network if they logged into the site in the last 28 days from our time of measurement in May 2011 and had at least one Facebook friend. We note that this definition is not precisely Facebook’s ordinary definition of active user, and therefore some of our statistics differ slightly from company statistics

span.label: 'six degrees of separation' - MILGRAM'S PHRASE ON A DIFFERENT INSTRUMENT: the original is letter-forwarding chains among Americans, this is shortest paths in a friendship graph, and the paper says the phenomenon is here SEEN in Facebook rather than claiming the two measurements are the same
span.quote: Short path lengths between individuals, the so-called “six degrees of separation” found by Stanley Milgram’s experiments investigating the social network of the United States [26], are here seen in Facebook on a global scale

span.label: the local clustering coefficient - READ AS A PERCENTAGE OF FRIEND PAIRS: an average coefficient of 0.14 for users with 100 friends is glossed as 14% of a median user's friend pairs being friends themselves, so an average over users is reported as a fact about a median one
span.quote: for users with 100 friends, the average local clustering coefficient is 0.14, indicating that for a median user, 14% of all their friend pairs are themselves friends

span.label: replicates → the small-world / six-degrees-of-separation phenomenon (Milgram)
span.quote: the average distance between pairs of users was 4.7

span.label: replicates → Stanley Milgram's 'six degrees of separation' experiments [26]
span.quote: Short path lengths between individuals, the so-called “six degrees of separation” found by Stanley Milgram’s experiments investigating the social network of the United States [26], are here seen in Facebook on a global scale.

span.label: extends → Feld's friendship paradox ('your friends have more friends than you') [30]
span.quote: This phenomena has been discussed at length by Feld [30], and Facebook displays the effect on a grand scale.

span.label: builds-on → Watts and Strogatz's small-world networks [44]
span.quote: Many other empirical networks, social and non-social, have also been observed with these characteristics, and Watts and Strogatz called networks with these properties ‘smallworld networks’ [44].

span.label: short path lengths —same-as→ degrees of separation
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — Q-558, 2026-08-15: READ THIS EDGE WITH senses[1]: the sense on this record that quotes the SAME SENTENCE says these are two different measurements: 'Milgram's phrase on a different instrument - the original is letter-forwarding chains among Americans, this is shortest paths in a friendship graph'. A path length in a friendship graph and a chain of acquaintances who forwarded a letter are not the same quantity. The type is left as it stands pending the wider decision about what `same-as` asserts; this note exists so the two are read together.
span.quote: Short path lengths between individuals, the so-called “six degrees of separation” found by Stanley Milgram’s experiments investigating the social network of the United States [26], are here seen in Facebook on a global scale

span.label: active user —contrasted-with→ hubs
span.quote: The small population of users with abnormally high degrees, sometimes called hubs in the networks literature, have degrees far larger than the average or median Facebook user

span.label: 721 million — size of the Facebook graph analysed (May 2011)
span.quote: a network then comprised of 721 million active users. To our knowledge, this is the largest social network ever analyzed.

span.label: 99.91% — fraction of users in the single large connected component
span.quote: the social network is nearly fully connected, with 99.91% of individuals belonging to a single large connected component

span.label: 4.7 — average distance between Facebook users (May 2011) — four degrees
span.quote: The average distance between users on Facebook in May 2011 was 4.7

span.label: Although the graph is globally sparse, users local neighborhoods are surprisingly dense, and the graph shows clear assortativity by demographic and network properties.
span.quote: while the Facebook graph as a whole is clearly sparse, the graph neighborhoods of users contain surprisingly dense structure

span.label: user degree / neighborhood locality
span.quote: the average local clustering coefficient and degeneracy of graph neighborhoods

span.label: global connectivity / average path length / assortativity
span.term: global connectivity / average path length / assortativity
span.quote: The average distance between users on Facebook in May 2011 was 4.7

span.label: assortativity
span.quote: we characterize the assortativity patterns present in the graph by studying the basic demographic and network properties of users

span.label: connected component
span.quote: 99.91% of individuals belonging to a single large connected component

span.label: correlation
span.quote: For the Facebook network, r = 0.226, displaying positive correlations with similar magnitude to other social graphs.

span.quote: For example, for users with 100 friends, the average local clustering coefficient is 0.14, indicating that for a median user, 14% of all their friend pairs are themselves friends.

span.label: sample-size
span.quote: According to our definition of active, the population of active Facebook users consisted of around n = 721 million individuals at the time of our measurements.

span.label: statistical-significance
span.quote: Restricting the comparison to individuals age 13 or more and with access to the internet (the set of individuals eligible to have Facebook accounts) would put this percentage significantly higher.
